sourceLines.text: At Westbridge University, a broken lamp or damaged pair of headphones no longer
has to go straight into the rubbish. Once a month, students bring faulty objects to
the Campus Repair Café. The café is not a business, and nobody pays for the repairs.
Instead, volunteers with practical skills sit beside the owners and help them discover
what went wrong.
________________ (See question 3.)  The idea began when engineering student Lina
Haddad noticed how many useful objects were being thrown away in her residence
hall. Some had only a loose wire or a missing screw. Lina invited three friends to
meet in an empty classroom with a few basic tools. During their first afternoon, they
repaired twelve of the nineteen items that people brought in. The volunteers do not
simply take an object away and return it later. They explain each step because the
main aim is to share knowledge. Visitors learn how to open a device safely, identify
a simple fault and decide whether a professional repair is needed. Even when an
item cannot be saved, its owner usually understands why. As the event became better
known, the organisers created a booking system. Simple repairs can be attempted at
any table, but jobs involving electricity are given to experienced volunteers. The
team  also  keeps  a  record  of  common  faults.  Loose  charging  connections,  broken
switches and damaged cables appear regularly, so volunteers prepare suitable tools
before each session begins.
Safety remains more important than the number of successful repairs. Volunteers
refuse to open equipment containing dangerous batteries, and they never promise
that every object can be fixed. When a repair needs a special part, they help the
owner identify it and explain what to tell a professional. This honest approach has
helped visitors develop realistic expectations. The project has started influencing
what  students  buy.  Several  visitors  now  check  whether  replacement  parts  are
available before choosing a new device. Others borrow equipment they expect to use
only once. These decisions are not required by the café, but they show that repair
lessons can affect behaviour outside the monthly event. New volunteers first observe
an experienced helper and practise on objects that have already been discarded. This
prevents their training from putting a visitor's property at risk. They also learn how
to  explain  a  technical  problem  in  plain  language,  since  good  communication  is
almost as important as knowing how to use the tools.
The café has also become a social event. Students from different departments work
together, drink tea and exchange advice. Lina hopes that the project will encourage
people to value their possessions for longer. She knows the café will not solve the
world's waste problem, but she believes small changes in everyday habits can still
have a useful effect.

sourceLines.text: Mangroves  grow  where  most  trees  cannot  survive:  in  salty  water  along  warm
coastlines. Their roots rise above the wet ground and form a thick natural barrier
between  land  and  sea.  At  first  sight,  a  mangrove  forest  may  look  untidy,  but  it
performs several jobs that are extremely valuable to both people and wildlife.
________________ (See question 3.)  During storms, strong waves lose some of their
energy as they pass through the roots. This can reduce damage to homes and roads
near the coast. The roots also hold soil in place, so less of it is carried away by the
sea. For coastal communities, a healthy mangrove forest can therefore provide an
important form of protection.
Mangroves are also busy living spaces. Young fish hide among the roots until they
are
large enough to move into open water. Birds rest in the branches, while crabs and
other  small  creatures  feed  in  the  mud  below.  Local  fishing  can  suffer  when
mangroves
disappear because many sea animals depend on them during the early part of their
lives. The forests can support people in less obvious ways too. Some communities
guide  visitors  through  mangrove  channels,  while  others  collect  natural  products
without  removing  whole  trees.  These  activities  can  provide  income  and  give
residents a direct reason to protect the forest. If too much wood or wildlife is taken,
however, the system quickly becomes less valuable.
Scientists monitor restored areas for several years rather than judging success after
one planting season. They count surviving trees, examine soil and observe whether
fish and birds return. A site with fewer planted trees may eventually perform better
than a crowded site if water can move naturally and young roots have enough space
to
develop. Education is another part of restoration. School groups visit young forests
to
measure  trees  and  remove  rubbish  trapped  among  the  roots.  The  activity  helps
students
understand why a muddy coastal area is not empty land. Some later return with their
families, spreading awareness beyond the classroom.
Protection on land is important as well. Plastic waste and polluted water can enter a
mangrove forest from streets and rivers. Planting new trees will achieve little if
these wider problems continue. Successful programmes therefore connect coastal
restoration  with  better  waste  collection  and  water  management  in  nearby
communities.
In  some  places,  mangroves  were  removed  to  make  room  for  buildings,  farms  or
tourist
developments. Today, communities are planting them again. However, restoration is
not as simple as placing young trees anywhere along the shore. Workers must first
study  the  movement  of  water  and  choose  suitable  species.  If  the  conditions  are
wrong, even thousands of new trees may fail to survive.

sourceLines.text: For many years, travellers in Europe could board a train in one city, sleep through
the night and wake up in another country. Later, cheap flights became more common,
and  several  night-train  services  disappeared.  Recently,  however,  some  railway
companies have brought them back, and passengers are showing renewed interest.
________________ (See question 4.) One reason is convenience. A night train carries
travellers while they sleep, so they do not lose most of a day on the journey. It also
takes them from one city centre to another. Airports are often far outside cities, and
passengers must arrive early for security checks. On a train, the start and end of the
trip can feel simpler. Environmental concerns are another factor. Trains generally
produce  less  pollution  per  passenger  than  planes,  especially  on  medium-length
journeys. Some travellers are willing to spend more or travel longer if their choice
has  a  smaller  environmental  effect.  Railway  companies have  responded  by
introducing  routes  that  connect  several  major  cities.  Design  also  influences  the
experience. Some new services offer private cabins with beds and showers, while
others use simple shared compartments. Families may value a door they can close,
but solo travellers often choose a cheaper shared space. Railway companies must
balance comfort with price because luxurious cabins take up room that could carry
more passengers.
International  services  create  another  challenge.  Trains  may  cross  borders  where
railway systems use different rules, ticketing systems or equipment. A delay in one
country  can  affect  the  entire  route.  Companies  therefore  need  close  cooperation,
especially when passengers buy one journey involving trains operated by several
organisations. Booking can be confusing when several types of accommodation are
offered. A passenger may need to choose between a seat, a shared sleeping space
and  a  private  cabin.  Clear  photographs  and  explanations  are  important  because
travellers cannot easily change rooms after the journey has begun. Arrival time also
shapes passengers' opinions. Reaching a city very early saves daylight hours, but
hotels may not yet allow guests into their rooms. Some stations have responded with
luggage  storage,  showers  and  early  cafés.  These  small  services  can  make  the
difference between a tiring arrival and a useful first morning.
Night trains still have disadvantages. A private sleeping cabin can be costly, while
the  cheapest  seats  may  be  uncomfortable  for  a  full  night.  Delays  can  also  cause
problems  for  passengers  with  further  connections.  Even  so,  supporters  say  the
experience is part of the attraction: they can watch the landscape change, meet other
travellers and arrive directly in the heart of a new city.

sourceLines.text: Students sometimes reduce their sleep before an important exam because extra study
time seems more valuable. However, staying awake late can work against the goal of
remembering more. Sleep is not simply a period when the brain switches off. While we
rest, it continues to process information gathered during the day.
________________  (See  question  4.)  One  important  process is  the  strengthening  of
memories. After a person learns new material, the memory is still weak and can be
easily lost. During sleep, the brain appears to organise this information and connect it
with  knowledge  already  stored.  A  good  night's  sleep  after  studying  can  therefore
support later recall.
Lack  of  sleep  also  affects  attention.  A  tired  student  may  read  the  same  paragraph
several  times  without  fully  understanding  it.  In  class,  the  student  may  miss  a  key
instruction or make a simple mistake. This means that an extra hour of late-night study
is not always as productive as it appears. The quality of sleep matters as well as the
number of hours. Noise, uncomfortable temperatures and repeated waking can prevent
a person from moving normally through different stages of sleep. Someone may spend
a long time in
bed but still feel tired in the morning. A calm and reasonably dark room can support
more restful sleep.
Caffeine can complicate the situation. Coffee or energy drinks may make a tired student
feel more alert for a while, but consuming them late in the day can delay sleep. The
student may then depend on more caffeine the following morning. Breaking this cycle
often requires gradual changes rather than one perfect night. Short naps can sometimes
improve alertness, but timing is important. A brief early-afternoon nap may help a tired
learner continue working. Sleeping for too long or too late, however, can make it harder
to  fall  asleep  at  night.  Naps  work  best  as  occasional  support,  not  as  a  permanent
replacement for regular sleep. Students often notice tiredness only when they begin
making mistakes. Keeping a simple record of sleep, concentration and mood for one
week can reveal patterns. The record does not need to be complicated. Its purpose is to
connect daily choices with performance and identify one realistic habit to change.
Experts usually recommend a regular sleep schedule rather than a single long sleep
after several short nights. Students can also plan difficult work earlier in the evening
and stop using bright screens shortly before bed. These habits do not remove the need
to study, but they help the brain make better use of the work already completed.

sourceLines.text: Early bicycles looked very different from the machines people ride today. Some had
no pedals, so riders pushed their feet against the ground. Later designs included pedals
attached directly to the front wheel. Inventors kept changing the bicycle because each
version solved one problem but often created another.
________________ (See question 4.)  One famous design had a huge front wheel and a
very small back wheel. The large wheel allowed the bicycle to travel farther with each
turn  of  the  pedals,  making  it faster.  However,  the  rider  sat  high above  the  ground.
Falling  was  common  and  could  be  serious,  so  the  machine  was  not  suitable  for
everyone. A major improvement came when designers used two wheels of a similar size
and connected the pedals to the back wheel with a chain. Riders could sit lower, which
made the bicycle safer and easier to control. Air-filled rubber tyres later made journeys
more comfortable on rough roads. The new design changed who could ride. A lower
seat  made  starting  and  stopping  less  frightening,  and  different  frame  shapes  made
bicycles  practical  for  a  wider  range  of  clothing.  As  production  increased,  prices
gradually fell. Bicycles became useful not only for sport but also for travelling to work,
carrying small goods and visiting nearby places.
Road conditions encouraged further improvements. Early tyres were solid and passed
every  shock  from  the  road  to  the  rider.  Air-filled  tyres  provided  a  softer  journey,
although they introduced the possibility of punctures. Better brakes and gears later
helped riders control speed on hills, making bicycles more useful in areas that were
not flat. Standard parts made repairs easier. When bicycles used completely different
designs, a damaged component could be difficult to replace. As common wheel sizes,
chains and fittings developed, repair shops could keep useful parts in stock. Owners
no longer needed to return every bicycle to its original maker. The bicycle continued
to  change  for  different  purposes.  Racing  models  became  light  and  narrow,  while
working bicycles gained stronger frames and racks. Mountain bicycles later used wide
tyres and improved suspension. These forms look different, yet they all depend on the
safer basic arrangement developed earlier.
By  combining  these  ideas,  the  bicycle  reached  a  basic  shape  that  is  still  familiar.
Modern bicycles use lighter materials and improved brakes, and some include electric
motors. Yet the central design—two similar wheels, a chain and pedals—has remained
remarkably successful. Its history shows how inventions often develop through many
small improvements rather than one perfect idea.

sourceLines.text: When an old factory, station or warehouse is no longer used for its original purpose, a
city must  decide what  to do with it.  Demolition may seem  like  the  easiest  answer.
However, some architects prefer adaptive reuse: keeping much of the existing building
while giving it a completely new function.
________________  (See  question  4.)  Reusing  a  building  can  protect  local  history.  A
former factory may remind residents of industries that once provided thousands of jobs.
Keeping its walls, signs or machinery allows part of that story to remain visible. The
building can then become apartments, offices, a market or an arts centre. There can
also  be  environmental  benefits.  Demolition  produces  large  amounts  of  waste,  and
constructing a replacement requires new concrete, steel and glass. Reuse saves at least
some of the energy and materials already contained in the original structure. It may
also bring activity back to an empty neighbourhood.
Before design work begins, specialists investigate the building carefully. They study
original plans, test materials and identify features that must be protected. Discovering
a hidden weakness early may prevent an expensive surprise later. The investigation
also reveals parts of the building that can safely be removed to create light, entrances
or shared spaces. Local opinion can shape the project. Residents may support reuse but
disagree  about  the  new  function.  Luxury  apartments,  for  example,  may  preserve  a
historic  wall  while  offering  little  benefit  to  the  wider  community.  Public  meetings
allow planners to hear these concerns, although it is rarely possible to satisfy every
group completely.
Building rules may require creative solutions. A historic staircase can be beautiful but
too narrow for modern safety standards. Architects might preserve it for appearance
while adding a new escape route elsewhere. Successful reuse depends on respecting
important  features  without  ignoring  the  needs  of  present-day  users.  The  work  can
uncover unexpected stories. Names scratched into a wall, old signs or unusual repairs
may reveal how earlier workers used the space. Project teams sometimes photograph
these details before construction continues. Even if everything cannot remain visible,
a record can be displayed in the renewed building.
Nevertheless, adaptive reuse is not always cheap or simple. Old buildings may contain
unsafe materials, have weak floors or lack modern systems for heating and electricity.
Architects must work within an existing shape instead of beginning with empty land.
The best projects accept these  restrictions and turn unusual features—such as high
ceilings or thick brick walls—into part of the building's new character.

sourceLines.text: Growing vegetables in a desert is difficult because strong sunlight, high temperatures
and dry winds cause water to disappear quickly. Some farms are using shade houses to
create a more suitable environment. Unlike a fully closed greenhouse, a shade house
is
covered with material that blocks part of the sunlight while still allowing air to move
through.
________________ (See question 4.) The cover lowers the temperature around the plants
and reduces the amount of water lost from leaves and soil. Drip pipes deliver small
amounts of water directly to the roots instead of wetting the whole field. Together,
these methods allow farmers to grow crops with less water than traditional open-field
farming would require.
Choosing the correct level of shade is important. If the material blocks too much light,
plants may grow slowly or produce fewer vegetables. If it blocks too little, the heat
remains a problem. Farmers often test different covers and observe plant growth before
using one across a large area. Farmers also pay attention to the time of year. A cover
that works well in the hottest months may provide unnecessary shade during cooler
weather. Some structures use material that can be rolled back or replaced. This allows
growers to change conditions without rebuilding the entire shade house for each season.
Information from simple sensors can support decisions. Devices measure temperature,
soil moisture and humidity at different points inside the structure. Farmers compare
these  readings  with  plant  growth  and  water  use.  Technology  does  not  replace
experience,  but  it  can  reveal  a  dry  area  or  rising  temperature  before  the  damage
becomes  clearly  visible.  Crop  selection  remains  important.  Leafy  vegetables  may
respond differently from tomatoes or cucumbers, and a variety successful in one region
may struggle in another.
Farmers begin with small trials so that a failure does not waste an entire season's water,
labour and growing space.
Workers  need training to notice early signs  of stress. Leaves that change  colour or
shape may indicate excessive heat, insufficient water or disease. Responding quickly
can  save  a  crop,  but  adding  more  water  is  not  always  the  correct  answer.  Careful
observation prevents one problem from creating another. Shade houses are not a perfect
answer. They cost money to build, covers can be damaged by strong winds, and pests
may still enter through open sides. Yet  they offer farmers a  flexible  middle choice
between outdoor fields and expensive closed greenhouses. In regions where every drop
of water matters, that balance can make local food production more practical.

sourceLines.text: Most bread rises because a baker adds commercial yeast. Sourdough uses a different
method: a starter made from flour and water. The starter contains wild yeast and helpful
bacteria from the flour and surrounding environment. Together, these living organisms
produce gases and acids that change the dough.
________________  (See  question  4.)  Creating a  starter  takes  patience. A baker mixes
flour and water, then regularly removes part of the mixture and adds fresh flour and
water. This is called feeding the starter. At first, its activity may be unpredictable, but
after several days it usually begins to rise and fall in a more regular pattern. When the
starter  is  active,  a  small  amount  is  mixed  with  more  flour,  water  and  salt  to  make
dough.  The  yeast  produces  gas,  which  becomes  trapped and  makes  the  bread  rise.
Bacteria create acids that give sourdough its particular flavour. The process is slower
than using commercial yeast and can change with room temperature.
Flour choice can change a starter. Whole-grain flour contains different nutrients and
microorganisms  from  highly  refined  flour,  while  water  temperature  influences  how
quickly activity develops. Bakers do not need laboratory equipment, but they benefit
from changing one factor at a time. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to understand why
the  starter  behaved  differently.  The  timing  of  bread-making  is  flexible  but  not
unlimited. Dough can develop more slowly in a cool room or faster in a warm one.
Bakers sometimes place it in a refrigerator to delay the process overnight. Learning to
recognise  the  correct  stage  is  more  reliable  than  following  the  clock  without
considering temperature and activity.
A  healthy  starter  usually  has  a  pleasantly  sour  smell,  but  unusual  colours  or  an
unpleasant  rotten  smell  can  signal  a  problem.  Bakers  learn  the  difference  between
normal change and contamination. When safety is uncertain, beginning again with clean
equipment  is  wiser  than  trying  to  rescue  a  doubtful  mixture.  Sharing  starters  also
spreads stories. A baker may describe a mixture as decades old, although its flour and
water have been replaced many times through feeding. What continues is the living
community and the routine of
care. The starter becomes a connection between kitchens rather than a fixed object.
A starter can remain alive for years if it is fed and stored correctly. Bakers sometimes
share part of theirs with friends, so one mixture may produce bread in many kitchens.
Although recipes provide useful measurements, experienced bakers also watch how the
dough feels and changes. Sourdough is therefore a combination of science, routine and
careful observation.

sourceLines.text: In the mountain village of San Isidro, homes are spread far apart and the nearest
electricity line ends many kilometres away. For years, families used candles or fuel
lamps  after  sunset.  The  lamps  provided  light,  but  the  fuel  was  costly,  produced
smoke and had to be carried up a difficult road.
________________ (See question 4.) A local organisation introduced small solar-light
systems. Each family received a panel for the roof, a battery and several efficient
lights. During the day, the panel charges the battery. At night, the stored energy
powers  the  lights for several  hours. Local technicians were trained to install  the
equipment and complete basic repairs.
The change affected daily routines. Children could read without sitting close to a
smoky lamp, and adults had more time for work inside the home. Families also made
fewer journeys to buy fuel. However, the systems did not provide enough electricity
for cookers or large machines, so residents had to understand their limits. Residents
decided together where outdoor lights would be most useful. They selected the path
to the water point and the area beside the community building. Shared lighting made
evening  movement  easier,  but  the  village  limited  the  number  of  lamps  so  that
maintenance  costs  would  remain  manageable.  Not  every  dark  path  could  be  lit
immediately.
Training  local  technicians  reduced  waiting  time  when  a  problem  occurred.  They
learned to test connections, replace damaged switches and explain correct battery
use.  More  complex  faults  were  reported  to  the  organisation.  This  division  of
responsibility meant that simple problems could be solved locally while specialist
support  remained  available.  Battery  care  was  included  in  community  meetings.
Families learned which devices could be connected and why completely emptying a
battery  too  often  shortened  its  life.  Clear  indicators  showed  how  much  power
remained. These lessons helped prevent accidental damage and made evening energy
use more predictable.
The  village  continues  to  record  faults  and  costs.  This  information  helps  leaders
decide when older parts should be replaced and whether more systems can be added.
It  also  gives  future  projects  realistic  evidence  about  expenses  after  installation,
which are sometimes missing from early plans. Maintenance became the project's
biggest test. Dust reduced the panels' performance, and some batteries eventually
needed replacement. The organisation therefore created a small monthly payment
plan for spare parts and trained additional technicians. The project succeeded not
simply because equipment was delivered, but because the village developed a way
to care for it over time.

sourceLines.text: Digital maps can show a person's exact position, suggest the fastest route and update
traffic information within seconds. With these advantages, a folded paper map may
appear old-fashioned. Yet hikers, emergency workers and some travellers continue to
carry one because paper offers strengths that electronic devices do not.
________________ (See question 4.)  A paper map does not require a battery or mobile
signal.  It can  be  opened  after  a  phone  has  lost  power  or  when  mountains  block
communication.  It  also  displays  a  wide  area  at  once.  This  broad  view  helps  users
understand how roads, rivers and towns connect instead of seeing only the next
instruction.
Using paper requires different skills. A reader must match symbols to real features,
understand  scale  and keep the map facing the correct direction. At first, this can be
slower than following a moving arrow on a screen. With practice, however, users build
a stronger mental picture of the area around them. Choosing the right paper map is
important. A road map may cover a large region but show little detail about walking
paths.  A  hiking  map  includes  height,  land  features  and  smaller  tracks,  although  it
covers a narrower area. Users should check the map's purpose, date and scale before
depending on it. Keeping a map protected is simple but necessary. Travellers may place
it in a clear waterproof case or fold only the section required for the day. They can
also mark planned routes lightly without hiding important symbols. These habits make
the map easier to use when weather is poor or a quick decision is needed.
Practising before an emergency is essential. A map kept at the bottom of a bag is not
useful if its owner cannot identify a current position. Hikers can develop confidence
on familiar routes by checking landmarks and predicting what they should see next
before  confirming  the  answer  digitally.  Groups  should  agree  on  a  route  rather  than
assume  one  person  has  all  the  information.  If  members  become  separated,  a  shared
understanding of meeting points and direction can reduce confusion. The map supports
communication because everyone can look at the same complete area together.
Paper maps have weaknesses. They can become wet, tear or show information that is
no longer current. For that reason, many experienced travellers combine both systems.
They use a digital map for live information and keep a recent paper map as a backup.
The question is not which form should disappear, but how each can support
the other.

sourceLines.text: North Valley University has buildings spread across a large campus. Walking from the
residence  halls  to  the  engineering  laboratories  can  take  twenty-five  minutes,  while
driving creates parking and traffic problems. To offer another choice, the university
introduced a bicycle-sharing scheme with stations beside major buildings.
________________ (See question 4.) Students register through the university
application and unlock a bicycle by scanning a code. The first thirty minutes of each
journey are free, which is long enough for most trips across campus. A small fee is
charged after that time to encourage users to return bicycles instead of keeping them
all day.
The first month revealed several difficulties. Bicycles accumulated near lecture halls
in the morning but were needed near the residence halls. Some stations became empty
while  others  were  completely  full.  A  transport  team  now  moves  bicycles  between
stations, and the application shows users where a bicycle or an empty return space is
available. Maintenance workers inspect bicycles regularly. They check brakes, tyres,
lights and seat adjustments, while users can report a problem through the application.
A bicycle marked as damaged cannot be borrowed until it has been examined. Quick
reporting matters because one unsafe bicycle could reduce trust in the entire scheme.
The university is also studying who uses the service. Early information suggests that
students living on campus borrow bicycles more often than staff and daily visitors.
Planners may add stations near car parks and bus stops to make the system useful to
those groups. Any expansion will be tested before a large number of new bicycles is
purchased. Weather strongly affects demand. Use falls during extreme heat or heavy
rain and rises on mild days. The transport team studies these changes before scheduling
maintenance,  since  a  quiet  period  is  a  good  time  to  remove  several  bicycles  for
inspection without leaving stations empty.
Students have suggested improvements such as baskets, additional lighting and lower
seats for shorter riders. The university cannot introduce every request immediately. It
first considers cost, safety and whether the change would help enough users. Small
trials allow feedback before equipment is fitted across the whole fleet.
Safety remains important. The university added marked cycle paths and reduced vehicle
speeds in busy areas It also offers short training sessions. Helmets are available at
several stations, although their use is not  compulsory. The scheme has not removed
every traffic problem, but surveys suggest that many students now choose a bicycle for
short journeys that they previously made by car.

sourceLines.text: Artificial intelligence is often described as if a machine were thinking exactly like a person.
In reality, many AI systems learn by finding patterns in large collections of examples. A
program  that  identifies  birds  in  photographs  may  study  thousands  of  images
marked with the correct species names. These examples help it connect shapes, colours and
textures with particular labels. The system does not understand a bird in the human sense;
it  calculates  which  answer  is  most  likely  based  on  relationships  found  during
training.
________________ (See question 4.) Engineers first choose data that represents the task they
want the system to perform. They may divide it into a training set and a separate testing
set. During training, the model makes predictions, compares them with the correct answers
and  adjusts  its  internal  calculations.  This  cycle  happens  many  times.  Gradually,  useful
patterns become stronger while unhelpful ones become weaker. The amount of data matters,
but  quality  is  equally  important  because  inaccurate  or  narrow  examples  can  teach  the
system the wrong lesson.
Testing reveals whether the model can handle examples it has never seen before. A system
may perform well on its training data yet fail in real situations. For instance, an image
model  trained  mainly  on  bright  daytime  photographs  may  struggle  at  night.  AI  can
also become  biased when some groups or situations are poorly represented in the data.
Researchers  therefore  examine  errors,  compare  results  across  groups  and  improve  the
information used to train the model.
Even a highly accurate system needs human oversight. AI can process information quickly,
but it may give a confident answer without recognising that the situation is unusual. People
must decide where the technology is appropriate, check important decisions and protect
private information. Artificial intelligence is most useful when its strengths and limits are
understood. It is not a magical replacement for human judgement; it is a powerful tool
whose results depend on data, design and responsible use.

sourceLines.text: Coral reefs may look like colourful underwater rocks, but they are built by living animals.
A coral  colony contains  thousands  of  tiny  polyps,  each  with  a  soft  body  and  a  mouth
surrounded  by  tentacles.  The  polyps  produce  hard  skeletons  of  calcium  carbonate.  As
generations grow on top of older skeletons, enormous reef structures slowly form. Although
reefs  cover  only  a  small  part  of  the  ocean  floor,  they  provide  food  and  shelter  for  a
remarkable variety of marine life.
________________ (See question 4.) Most reef-building corals depend on a close partnership
with microscopic algae living inside their tissues. The algae use sunlight to produce energy
and share much of  it with the coral. In return, the coral provides a protected home and
materials the algae need. This relationship helps corals grow in clear tropical water where
nutrients are limited. It also gives many corals their colour. Without the algae, the coral
animal is nearly transparent, and its white skeleton becomes visible through its body.
When water remains unusually warm, the partnership can break down. Stressed corals push
out their algae and become pale in a process called  bleaching. A bleached coral is not
necessarily dead, but it  has lost an important source of energy. If temperatures return to
normal soon, algae may return and the coral can recover. If the stress continues, disease
and  death  become  more  likely.  Pollution,  destructive  fishing  and  changes  in  ocean
chemistry can add further pressure.
Reef protection therefore requires action at several levels. Local communities can reduce
pollution, manage fishing and prevent physical damage from boats or careless vis itors.
These steps make reefs stronger, but  they cannot fully protect coral from rising ocean
temperatures.  Wider  reductions  in  greenhouse-gas  emissions  are  also
necessary. Scientists are testing heat-tolerant corals and restoration methods, yet no single
technique  can  replace  a  healthy  climate  and  well-managed  coast.  The  future  of  reefs
depends  on  protecting  both  the  coral  animals  and  the  conditions  supporting  their
partnership.

sourceLines.text: Chocolate begins with the seeds of the cacao tree, a tropical plant native to the Americas.
Long before chocolate became a sweet bar, ancient Mesoamerican societies prepared cacao
as a bitter drink and valued the beans in trade and ceremonies. Europeans later added sugar
and changed the way cacao was consumed. Demand spread, and cacao was cultivated in
other tropical regions. Today, West Africa produces much of the world's supply, although
the crop still requires the warm, wet conditions found near the equator.
________________  (See  question  4.)  Cacao pods grow directly from the trunk and large
branches of the tree. Farmers cut ripe pods by hand because machines could damage the
tree or nearby flowers. Inside each pod, beans are surrounded by white fruit pulp. Workers
remove  them  and  place  the  mixture  in  boxes  or  piles  covered  with
leaves.  During  fermentation,  natural  chemical  changes  reduce  bitterness  and  begin
creating the flavours associated with chocolate. Without  this stage, the beans would not
develop the familiar taste that consumers expect.
After fermentation, the beans are dried in the sun to lower their moisture. They are then
packed and transported to a factory, where they are cleaned, roasted and opened. Roasting
develops flavour, while removing the shells leaves small pieces called cacao nibs. The nibs
are ground into a thick liquid known as cocoa mass. Manufacturers mix it with different
amounts of sugar, cocoa butter and sometimes milk. These choices determine whether the
final product becomes dark, milk or white chocolate.
The mixture is refined until it feels smooth, then heated and cooled carefully in a process
called tempering. Properly tempered chocolate has a shiny surface and breaks with a clear
snap.  Production,  however,  involves  more  than  flavour.  Farmers  may  face
low  incomes,  crop  disease  and  changing  weather.  Some  companies  and  certification
programmes aim to improve working conditions and support more sustainable farming. A
chocolate bar is therefore the result of history, agriculture, chemistry, transport and many
people's labour.

options.text: Chance plays no role when players prepare carefully.
Penalty success depends on physical, strategic and psychological factors.
Physical strength is the only useful ability in football.
One strategy can guarantee success in every penalty.

sourceLines.text: A football penalty kick appears simple: one player shoots from a fixed spot while one
goalkeeper  protects  the  goal.  Yet  the  situation  involves  speed,  judgement  and  intense
pressure.  From  the  moment  the  ball  is  kicked,  it  can  reach  the  goal  in  less  than  half
a second. The goalkeeper may not have enough time to wait, see the ball’s direction and
then react. Instead, both players use small clues and planned strategies to improve their
chances in a contest that is partly physical and partly psychological.
________________ (See question 4.) Goalkeepers often study a shooter's previous penalties
before an important match. They look for repeated choices, such as a preference for one
corner. During the kick, they may watch the angle of the shooter's body, the position of the
supporting foot or the direction of the hips. These signals can help them anticipate where
the ball will travel. However, experienced players try to disguise their intention or wait for
the goalkeeper to move before choosing a side.
Researchers  have  examined  whether  a  goalkeeper  should  dive  or  remain  in  the  centre.
Because  most  penalties  are  directed  towards  a  corner,  diving  is  usually  reasonable.
Nevertheless, some shots travel down the middle because the player expects movement.
Goalkeepers may also feel pressure to make a visible action; standing still can look passive
even when it is a planned decision. Statistics can guide a strategy, but a single kick remains
uncertain because each player's behaviour influences the other's
choice.
The shooter's mental control is equally important. A crowded stadium, the score and the
importance of the match can increase anxiety. Players often develop a routine involving
breathing,  a  fixed  number  of  steps  and  a  clear  target.  A  consistent  routine
helps direct attention toward the action rather than the possible result. Penalties show why
sport cannot be explained by physical ability alone. Preparation, observation, probability
and emotional control all contribute, while chance still ensures that no strategy succeeds
every time.
